name: 1 Corinthians

overview.author: The apostle Paul, with Sosthenes (1:1).
overview.date: About AD 53–55, from Ephesus during Paul’s third missionary journey (16:8).
overview.audience: The church in Corinth, a wealthy, diverse, and morally permissive Greek port city, which Paul founded (Acts 18).
overview.setting: Reports from Chloe’s household and a letter from the church raised problems: factions, immorality, lawsuits, marriage questions, food offered to idols, disorder in worship, spiritual gifts, and doubts about the resurrection.
overview.purpose: To correct divisions and sin, answer the church’s questions, and center everything on Christ crucified and risen, with love as the more excellent way.
overview.structure: Divisions and the wisdom of the cross (1–4), moral problems (5–6), answers about marriage, idol food, and worship (7–14), the resurrection (15), and closing instructions (16).

items.title: Food offered to idols and freedom
Christ raised and our future bodies

themes.title: The Cross
themes.text: God’s wisdom looks foolish to the world but is the power of God.

themes.title: Unity
themes.text: Christ is not divided; leaders are servants.

themes.title: Holiness
themes.text: Believers are God’s temple, bought with a price, called to flee sexual immorality.

themes.title: Christian Freedom and Love
themes.text: Freedom is limited by love for others’ consciences.

themes.title: The Body of Christ
themes.text: Many members, many gifts, one Spirit.

themes.title: Love
themes.text: Love is patient and kind and never ends (13).

christInBook.text: Christ crucified is the power and wisdom of God.
Christ became our wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption.
Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.
Christ is the firstfruits of those raised from the dead.
The last Adam became a life-giving spirit.

crossReferences.note: Paul founds the church in Corinth.

reflection: Where do you see divisions over personalities or preferences, and how can you promote unity?
How does “you are not your own” shape how you treat your body?
How might your freedom need to be limited by love for someone else (8:13)?
Read 1 Corinthians 13:4–7 inserting your name. Where do you fall short?
How does the resurrection give meaning to your labor (15:58)?

chapterList.title: The Word of the Cross
chapterList.summary: Paul thanks God for the Corinthians’ gifts. He appeals against divisions: “I follow Paul,” “I follow Apollos.” “Is Christ divided?” The word of the cross is folly to the perishing but the power of God to the saved. God chose the foolish and weak to shame the wise and strong, so no one may boast except in the Lord.
questions: Why were the Corinthians divided?
Why does the cross seem foolish to the world?
Why does God choose the weak (1:27–29)?

chapterList.title: Spirit-Taught Wisdom
chapterList.summary: Paul came not with eloquence but resolved to know nothing “except Jesus Christ and him crucified,” so faith would rest on God’s power. God’s hidden wisdom is revealed by the Spirit. The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit, but “we have the mind of Christ.”
questions: Why did Paul avoid relying on eloquence?
What has God prepared for those who love Him (2:9)?
How does the Spirit reveal God’s truth (2:10–16)?

chapterList.title: God’s Field and God’s Temple
chapterList.summary: The Corinthians are still worldly, divided over leaders. Paul planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. Each builder must take care how he builds on the foundation, Jesus Christ; work will be tested by fire. “You are God’s temple and God’s Spirit dwells in you.”
questions: Why are church leaders “only servants” (3:5)?
How will our work be tested (3:12–15)?
What does it mean that the church is God’s temple (3:16–17)?

chapterList.title: Servants of Christ
chapterList.summary: Leaders are servants and stewards, judged by the Lord, not human courts. Paul contrasts the Corinthians’ arrogance with the apostles’ suffering, “fools for Christ’s sake.” As their father in the faith, he urges them to imitate him and sends Timothy.
questions: What is required of stewards (4:2)?
How should we view others’ judgments of us (4:3–5)?
What does “What do you have that you did not receive?” teach (4:7)?

chapterList.title: Discipline in the Church
chapterList.summary: A man is living with his father’s wife, and the church is proud. Paul calls for his removal so that his spirit may be saved. A little leaven leavens the whole lump; Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed. Do not associate with a so-called brother who is sexually immoral or greedy.
questions: Why was tolerating this sin dangerous?
What is the goal of church discipline (5:5)?
How does Christ as our Passover lamb motivate holiness (5:7–8)?

chapterList.title: Bought with a Price
chapterList.summary: Believers are suing each other before unbelievers. Paul says it is better to be wronged. The unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom, “and such were some of you. But you were washed... sanctified... justified.” Flee sexual immorality. Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit; glorify God in your body.
questions: Why is suing a fellow believer before unbelievers wrong?
What hope does “such were some of you” (6:11) give?
How can you glorify God in your body (6:19–20)?

chapterList.title: Marriage and Singleness
chapterList.summary: Paul answers questions about marriage. Husbands and wives should not deprive each other. Believers should not divorce, and if an unbelieving spouse leaves, the believer is not bound. Each should lead the life the Lord assigned. Singleness allows undivided devotion to the Lord.
questions: How does Paul view marriage and sexual intimacy (7:3–5)?
What does 7:17–24 teach about contentment in your calling?
What advantages does singleness offer (7:32–35)?

chapterList.title: Knowledge and Love
chapterList.summary: On food offered to idols: knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. Idols are nothing, and there is one God and one Lord, Jesus Christ. But not all know this, and eating can wound a weaker brother’s conscience. “If food makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat.”
questions: Why does knowledge puff up while love builds up?
What does 8:6 teach about God and Christ?
Where might your freedom harm someone else?

chapterList.title: All Things to All People
chapterList.summary: Paul has rights as an apostle, including financial support, but gives them up for the gospel. “I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some.” He disciplines his body like an athlete for an imperishable wreath.
questions: Why did Paul give up his rights?
What does “all things to all people” look like today?
How does the athletic image apply to your spiritual life (9:24–27)?

chapterList.title: Flee Idolatry
chapterList.summary: Israel’s wilderness failures are examples: idolatry, immorality, testing God, grumbling. “Let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.” God provides a way of escape from temptation. Flee idolatry; you cannot share the Lord’s table and demons’ table. “Do all to the glory of God.”
questions: What lessons does Israel’s history teach (10:6–11)?
How does God help in temptation (10:13)?
What does doing everything for God’s glory look like (10:31)?

chapterList.title: Worship and the Lord’s Supper
chapterList.summary: Paul addresses head coverings, honoring God’s created order in worship. At the Lord’s Supper, divisions and selfishness shame the poor. Paul recounts Jesus’ institution: “Do this in remembrance of me.” Eating unworthily brings judgment; examine yourselves.
questions: What principles about honor in worship does Paul teach?
What was wrong with the Corinthians’ Lord’s Supper?
How should we prepare to take communion (11:27–32)?

chapterList.title: One Body, Many Members
chapterList.summary: There are varieties of gifts but the same Spirit, given for the common good. As a body has many parts, so the church is one body in Christ. Every member is needed; the weaker parts are indispensable. If one member suffers, all suffer together.
questions: Why does God give spiritual gifts (12:7)?
How does the body image fight both pride and inferiority?
What gifts has God given you to serve others?

chapterList.title: The Way of Love
chapterList.summary: Without love, gifts are nothing. “Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast.” Love bears, believes, hopes, and endures all things. Love never ends. Now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. “So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love.”
questions: Why are gifts worthless without love?
Which description of love in 13:4–7 is hardest for you?
Why is love the greatest (13:13)?

chapterList.title: Orderly Worship
chapterList.summary: Pursue love and desire prophecy, which builds up the church more than uninterpreted tongues. Everything in worship should be done for building up. God is not a God of confusion but of peace. “All things should be done decently and in order.”
questions: Why is building others up central to worship?
How should gifts be used in a gathering (14:26–33)?
How can your church gatherings reflect God’s order and peace?

chapterList.title: The Resurrection
chapterList.summary: Paul summarizes the gospel: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day, appearing to many. If Christ is not raised, our faith is futile. But He is the firstfruits. The dead will be raised with imperishable, spiritual bodies. “O death, where is your victory?” “Your labor is not in vain.”
questions: What are the essentials of the gospel (15:3–5)?
What would be lost if Christ had not risen (15:14–19)?
How does the resurrection affect your work (15:58)?

chapterList.title: The Collection and Final Charges
chapterList.summary: Paul instructs regular giving for the Jerusalem saints. He shares travel plans and commends Timothy and Apollos. “Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong. Let all that you do be done in love.” He ends, “Our Lord, come!”
questions: What principles of giving appear in 16:1–2?
How do 16:13–14 summarize Christian living?
What does “Maranatha” (“Our Lord, come!”) express?

tagline: Christ crucified for a divided, gifted, and struggling church
readingPlan: 16 chapters: one chapter a day takes 16 days; two a day takes about 8 days. For each chapter, read it on ESV.org, then come back here for the summary, questions, and your notes.
